data.title: Why You Might Be Interested In Mapfre, S.A. (BME:MAP) For Its Upcoming Dividend
data.description:
Some investors rely on dividends for growing their wealth, and if you're one of those dividend sleuths, you might be intrigued to know that Mapfre, S.A. (BME:MAP) is about to go ex-dividend in just three days. The ex-dividend date is two business days before a company's record date in most cases, which is the date on which the company determines which shareholders are entitled to receive a dividend. The ex-dividend date is of consequence because whenever a stock is bought or sold, the trade can take two business days or more to settle. In other words, investors can purchase Mapfre's shares before the 24th of November in order to be eligible for the dividend, which will be paid on the 26th of November.

The company's upcoming dividend is €0.0648 a share, following on from the last 12 months, when the company distributed a total of €0.18 per share to shareholders. Based on the last year's worth of payments, Mapfre has a trailing yield of 4.4% on the current stock price of €4.106. We love seeing companies pay a dividend, but it's also important to be sure that laying the golden eggs isn't going to kill our golden goose! So we need to check whether the dividend payments are covered, and if earnings are growing.

We've found 21 US stocks that are forecast to pay a dividend yield of over 6% next year. See the full list for free.

Dividends are typically paid from company earnings. If a company pays more in dividends than it earned in profit, then the dividend could be unsustainable. Fortunately Mapfre's payout ratio is modest, at just 27% of profit.

Companies that pay out less in dividends than they earn in profits generally have more sustainable dividends. The lower the payout ratio, the more wiggle room the business has before it could be forced to cut the dividend.

View our latest analysis for Mapfre

Click here to see the company's payout ratio, plus analyst estimates of its future dividends.

Have Earnings And Dividends Been Growing?

Stocks in companies that generate sustainable earnings growth often make the best dividend prospects, as it is easier to lift the dividend when earnings are rising. If earnings fall far enough, the company could be forced to cut its dividend. Fortunately for readers, Mapfre's earnings per share have been growing at 18% a year for the past five years.

Many investors will assess a company's dividend performance by evaluating how much the dividend payments have changed over time. In the past 10 years, Mapfre has increased its dividend at approximately 3.3% a year on average. It's good to see both earnings and the dividend have improved - although the former has been rising much quicker than the latter, possibly due to the company reinvesting more of its profits in growth.

To Sum It Up

From a dividend perspective, should investors buy or avoid Mapfre? Typically, companies that are growing rapidly and paying out a low fraction of earnings are keeping the profits for reinvestment in the business. Perhaps even more importantly - this can sometimes signal management is focused on the long term future of the business. Mapfre ticks a lot of boxes for us from a dividend perspective, and we think these characteristics should mark the company as deserving of further attention.

data.title: How Investors May Respond To Lennar (LEN) Misleading Disclosure Lawsuit
data.description:
• Lennar is facing a class action lawsuit filed in November 2026 that claims the company misled investors about its operating approach and the true purpose of the Millrose spin off, including how expenses were recorded and how affiliated transactions affected reported demand.
  • The complaint highlights an alleged use of Millrose to buy Lennar homes at above market prices and rent them at below market levels. If accurate, these practices would raise fundamental questions about how the homebuilder’s asset light model and demand trends were presented to shareholders.
  • This article examines how Lennar's investment narrative is challenged by alleged Millrose related home purchases used to support reported demand.
Spot fresh housing plays by comparing Lennar's legal and demand risks against a curated list of solid balance sheet and fundamentals (25 results) that are not relying on complex structures to support reported performance.

Lennar Investment Narrative Recap

To own Lennar, an investor needs to be comfortable with a homebuilder that relies heavily on an asset light model, tight build cycles and controlled homesites rather than a large land bank. The class action and Millrose allegations cut across that story because they question how land option costs and affiliated transactions intersect with the reported asset mix and demand.

In the short term, the key swing factor remains housing demand under high mortgage rates and Lennar’s ability to keep volumes moving with incentives while protecting already compressed 4.1% profit margins. The biggest risk now is that legal and regulatory scrutiny around Millrose raises compliance costs or constrains use of similar structures at a time when affordability pressure is already weighing on deliveries.

The lawsuit itself is the central development to focus on. Robbins LLP alleges Lennar capitalized expenses tied to land bank option agreements, rather than expensing them, and used Millrose to purchase homes above market prices while renting them below market levels. That critique goes directly to the analyst consensus narrative on Simply Wall St, which was built around the benefits of an asset and land light approach.

If the court process leads to tighter limits on affiliated land bank activity, the homebuilder may have less flexibility in how it balances reported margins, demand optics and land access. For you, the operational questions are whether Lennar can still sustain its volume focused production model, keep construction costs around US$80 per square foot under control and manage higher land and option fees without further pressure on earnings.

Lennar's analyst narrative points to revenues of US$40.6b and earnings of US$2.7b by 2029, based on assumed annual revenue growth of 8.3% and an earnings increase of about US$1.4b from US$1.3b today.

data.title: Companies Like Sky Metals (ASX:SKY) Are In A Position To Invest In Growth
data.description:
We can readily understand why investors are attracted to unprofitable companies. For example, although software-as-a-service business Salesforce.com lost money for years while it grew recurring revenue, if you held shares since 2005, you'd have done very well indeed. Nonetheless, only a fool would ignore the risk that a loss making company burns through its cash too quickly.

So, the natural question for Sky Metals (ASX:SKY) shareholders is whether they should be concerned by its rate of cash burn. In this article, we define cash burn as its annual (negative) free cash flow, which is the amount of money a company spends each year to fund its growth. The first step is to compare its cash burn with its cash reserves, to give us its 'cash runway'.

AI is about to change healthcare. These 20 stocks are working on everything from early diagnostics to drug discovery. The best part - they are all under $10bn in marketcap - there is still time to get in early.

Does Sky Metals Have A Long Cash Runway?

You can calculate a company's cash runway by dividing the amount of cash it has by the rate at which it is spending that cash. As at June 2026, Sky Metals had cash of AU$18m and no debt. Looking at the last year, the company burnt through AU$11m. So it had a cash runway of approximately 20 months from June 2026. Notably, analysts forecast that Sky Metals will break even (at a free cash flow level) in about 3 years. That means unless the company reduces its cash burn quickly, it may well look to raise more cash. Depicted below, you can see how its cash holdings have changed over time.

See our latest analysis for Sky Metals

How Is Sky Metals' Cash Burn Changing Over Time?

Sky Metals didn't record any revenue over the last year, indicating that it's an early stage company still developing its business. So while we can't look to sales to understand growth, we can look at how the cash burn is changing to understand how expenditure is trending over time. In fact, it ramped its spending strongly over the last year, increasing cash burn by 102%. That sort of spending growth rate can't continue for very long before it causes balance sheet weakness, generally speaking. Clearly, however, the crucial factor is whether the company will grow its business going forward. So you might want to take a peek at how much the company is expected to grow in the next few years.

How Hard Would It Be For Sky Metals To Raise More Cash For Growth?

While Sky Metals does have a solid cash runway, its cash burn trajectory may have some shareholders thinking ahead to when the company may need to raise more cash. Generally speaking, a listed business can raise new cash through issuing shares or taking on debt. Commonly, a business will sell new shares in itself to raise cash and drive growth. By comparing a company's annual cash burn to its total market capitalisation, we can estimate roughly how many shares it would have to issue in order to run the company for another year (at the same burn rate).

Since it has a market capitalisation of AU$119m, Sky Metals' AU$11m in cash burn equates to about 9.1% of its market value. That's a low proportion, so we figure the company would be able to raise more cash to fund growth, with a little dilution, or even to simply borrow some money.

So, Should We Worry About Sky Metals' Cash Burn?

Even though its increasing cash burn makes us a little nervous, we are compelled to mention that we thought Sky Metals' cash burn relative to its market cap was relatively promising. One real positive is that analysts are forecasting that the company will reach breakeven. Cash burning companies are always on the riskier side of things, but after considering all of the factors discussed in this short piece, we're not too worried about its rate of cash burn. STMicroelectronics Investment Narrative Recap

To be comfortable holding STMicroelectronics, you basically need to believe the company can turn its STM32 push, silicon carbide ambition and AI data center exposure into steadier earnings power. The fresh STM32 guidance does not change the near term swing factor, which is still execution on the long running manufacturing reshaping program.

The biggest operational risk right now stays the same. Fab migration and underloading are already weighing on gross margin, and any delay to closing older 150 millimeter and 200 millimeter facilities by around 2027 or 2028 could keep returns muted. Competitive and pricing pressure in China adds another layer of uncertainty for silicon carbide profitability, especially while one major segment is loss making and depends on a shift to 200 millimeter to improve.

The clearest announcement linked to this news is management's target to double STM32 revenue from 2025 to 2028, with potential market share of 25% to 30%. That ties directly into the existing catalysts around industrial automation, lean microcontroller inventories and AI related demand. It also frames STM32 not just as a workhorse MCU line but as a core compute platform for edge AI and data center adjacent workloads.

For you, the key question is execution. If STM32 really scales into AI data centers, automotive grade STM32A from 2028 and humanoid robotics, it could reinforce the thesis that new products, plus the footprint reshaping, eventually lift both growth and margins. If design wins, pricing or automotive qualifications disappoint, the risk is that the ambitious STM32 roadmap adds complexity without delivering enough earnings power to offset manufacturing and China related pressures.

STMicroelectronics' narrative projects US$20.3b revenue and US$3.7b earnings by 2029, which aligns with analyst assumptions of 15.7% yearly revenue growth and an increase in profit from US$466.0m today to US$3.7b. This represents an earnings increase of about 8x from current levels.

data.title: Netlist (NLST) Could Be 96% Below Fair Value Following AI Hardware And Edge AI Moves
data.description:
Netlist (NLST) has drawn fresh attention after revealing plans to pursue acquisitions in edge AI, reporting detailed third quarter results, and reshaping its leadership team around intellectual property and governance.

Recent trading tells a volatile story for Netlist. The share price has pulled back sharply with a 1-day share price return of down 5.43% and a 30-day share price return of down 28.72%, even though the year-to-date share price return is up 321.58% and the 1-year total shareholder return is very large at about 7x. Short-term pressure since the November earnings call and leadership changes suggests some investors are reassessing execution risk and acquisition plans, while the strong longer term total shareholder returns show how quickly sentiment has already swung on Netlist’s edge AI and IP monetization efforts.

Scan how other AI hardware and edge computing plays are reacting to the same demand shift by reviewing the curated 53 AI infrastructure stocks alongside Netlist.

The recent slide raises a simple tension: Are traders just cooling on Netlist’s edge AI story, or has the share price run ahead of what the current earnings and IP portfolio justify?

Preferred Price-to-Earnings of 17.4x: Is it justified?

Netlist closed at $4.18, and on a P/E of 17.4x it is being valued at a lower earnings multiple than many Electronic peers despite its edge AI focus and IP heavy model.

The P/E ratio relates the share price to earnings per share and gives you a shorthand view of how much investors are paying for current profitability. For a hardware and semiconductor oriented business like Netlist, this yardstick often reflects how durable the profit stream is seen to be in light of technology cycles and customer demand.

Analysts assessing Netlist’s scorecard will likely weigh that 17.4x multiple against several data points. Revenue is forecast to grow 62.4% per year according to the supplied estimates, NLST has recently become profitable, and the company is trading at a 96.4% discount to the SWS DCF model’s future cash flow value of $116.02 per share. That mix suggests the market is putting a relatively modest price on a forecast that screens as high growth and on an earnings base that has only just turned positive.

The comparison with peers is clear. NLST is described as good value on P/E versus both its peer set at 39.1x and the broader US Electronic industry at 24.7x. The market is valuing Netlist’s earnings at less than half the average multiple of close comparables and at a clear discount to the wider sector. This points to either a meaningful caution around execution or a potential valuation gap if the current profitability level and revenue forecasts are sustained.

Still, Netlist’s heavy reliance on a single Semiconductors segment, along with significant exposure to China and other overseas markets, could quickly challenge the current edge AI narrative.

Another view on Netlist’s value

There is a very different message coming from the SWS DCF model. At $4.18, Netlist is described as trading 96.4% below an estimated future cash flow value of $116.02 per share, which presents the stock as heavily undervalued if those long term cash assumptions prove realistic.

That kind of gap can cut both ways. It may suggest a large potential upside skew, or it may simply illustrate how sensitive a long dated forecast is to small changes in margins, legal outcomes, or capital needs.

data.title: What Do Eli Lilly (LLY) Vendor Hack And Canada Approval Mean Now?
data.description:
• Eli Lilly (NYSE: LLY) reported that a third-party vendor was hacked, exposing sensitive data tied to about 1.2 million patients.
  • The extortion group claiming responsibility is threatening to leak patient and prescriber information allegedly taken from Eli Lilly vendor systems.
  • Health Canada approved Mounjaro (tirzepatide) to reduce cardiovascular risk in adults with type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease.
  • The vendor cyberattack and the new Mounjaro cardiovascular label in Canada are changing how Eli Lilly’s risk and opportunity profile looks. Check out 3 other big wins that Eli Lilly investors should know about.

Consider widening your watchlist to include other companies exposed to similar themes by reviewing 33 elite gold producer stocks.

Eli Lilly operates as a large global pharmaceuticals manufacturer, discovering, developing, and marketing treatments across major regions including the US, Europe, China, and Japan. As a result, both data security standards and regulatory labelling decisions feed directly into how patients, doctors, and regulators view its core drug portfolio.

See how Eli Lilly's balance sheet measures up.

How could this Eli Lilly vendor hack affect the business financially?

The breach sits at a third party, yet it still brings potential costs for Eli Lilly around forensic work, vendor remediation and higher ongoing security spend. If regulators determine that protections for roughly 1.2 million patient records were inadequate, you could also see fines or tighter contractual requirements that raise compliance costs across the vendor base.

Does this Mounjaro cardiovascular approval in Canada change the Eli Lilly Narrative?

The Narrative leans on GLP 1 demand and access, and Health Canada’s decision gives Mounjaro an added cardiovascular indication that supports that core cardiometabolic story. It lines up with the catalyst around expanding obesity and diabetes franchises into broader disease areas, while legal and pricing risks from the Narrative still frame how much earnings power investors assume.

See how these catalysts shape Eli Lilly's path to a $1,463 fair value.

What number should investors watch next to judge the impact of these developments?

The key marker from here is any quantified disclosure of cyber related costs or provisions in upcoming earnings, set alongside reported revenue from tirzepatide products where management breaks out new cardiovascular indications in Canada. That pairing will show whether security and compliance spending is starting to eat into the performance margins analysts track for incretin drugs.

One more Eli Lilly question the headlines do not answer

Cyber issues and drug labels say a lot about today, but the real swing factor is where analysts think Eli Lilly’s earnings and cash flows end up a few years from now. See where analysts expect Eli Lilly to be in a few years.
